We note that $m=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $2m$ and $3m.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(2m,3m)=6m.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $6m,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3m+2}{2m}-\frac{m+2}{3m} & =1 \\ 6m\cdot (\frac{3m+2}{2m}-\frac{m+2}{3m}) & =6m\cdot (1) \\ 6m\cdot \frac{3m+2}{2m}-6m\cdot \frac{m+2}{3m} & =6m\cdot 1 \\ 3\cdot \cancel{2m}\cdot \frac{3m+2}{\cancel{2m}}-2\cdot \cancel{3m}\cdot \frac{m+2}{\cancel{3m}} & =6m \\ 3(3m+2)-2(m+2) & =6m\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $m,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}3(3m+2)-2(m+2) & =6m \\ 9m+6-2m-4 & =6m \\ 7m+2 & =6m \\ m & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $m=0$ as a solution. But since $m=-2\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $m=-2.$

questions.problem: Which value of $x$ satisfies the equation $\frac{x-4}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{2}{x}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We note that $x=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators ${x}^{2}$ and $x.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}({x}^{2},x)={x}^{2}.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by ${x}^{2},$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-4}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}} & =\frac{2}{x} \\ {x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{x-4}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2}{x}) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{x-4}{{x}^{2}})-{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{2}{x}) \\ \cancel{{x}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{x-4}{\cancel{{x}^{2}}})-\cancel{{x}^{2}}\cdot (\frac{1}{\cancel{{x}^{2}}}) & =x\cdot \cancel{x}\cdot (\frac{2}{\cancel{x}}) \\ (x-4)-1 & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $x,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x-4)-1 & =2x \\ x-5 & =2x \\ x & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $x=0$ as a solution. But since $x=-5\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $x=-5.$

questions.problem: Which value of $w$ satisfies the equation $\frac{2w-3}{3w}=\frac{1-w}{2w}-\frac{4w-1}{9w}?$
questions.worked_solution:
We note that $w=0$ cannot be a solution since division by $0$ is undefined. 

The equation has the denominators $2w,3w,$ and $9w.$ So first, we find the least common multiple (or $\text{LCM}$) of the denominators. We find that

$$
\text{LCM}(2w,3w,9w)=18w.
$$

So, we multiply both sides of the equation by $18w,$ and simplify: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2w-3}{3w} & =\frac{1-w}{2w}-\frac{4w-1}{9w} \\ 18w\cdot (\frac{2w-3}{3w}) & =18w\cdot (\frac{1-w}{2w}-\frac{4w-1}{9w}) \\ 18w\cdot (\frac{2w-3}{3w}) & =18w\cdot (\frac{1-w}{2w})+18w\cdot (-\frac{4w-1}{9w}) \\ 6\cdot 3w\cdot (\frac{2w-3}{3w}) & =9\cdot 2w\cdot (\frac{1-w}{2w})-2\cdot 9w\cdot (\frac{4w-1}{9w}) \\ 6\cdot \cancel{3w}\cdot (\frac{2w-3}{\cancel{3w}}) & =9\cdot \cancel{2w}\cdot (\frac{1-w}{\cancel{2w}})-2\cdot \cancel{9w}\cdot (\frac{4w-1}{\cancel{9w}}) \\ 6\cdot (2w-3) & =9\cdot (1-w)-2\cdot (4w-1)\end{aligned}
$$

We now have a linear equation in $w,$ and we can solve this using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}6(2w-3) & =9(1-w)-2(4w-1) \\ 12w-18 & =9-9w-8w+2 \\ 12w-18 & =11-17w \\ 12w+17w & =11+18 \\ 29w & =29 \\ w & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we recall that we cannot allow $w=0$ as a solution. But since $w=1\ne 0,$ we conclude that the solution is $w=1.$
